result:
The Persistence of Small Things

There is a particular kind of silence that exists only in the hour before dawn, when the world seems to hold its breath in anticipation of light returning. I have come to know this silence intimately over the years, not through any deliberate choice but through the slow accumulation of sleepless nights, of early mornings when waking felt more honest than pretending to rest. In these hours, I have watched the sky transition from the deep purple of bruised fruit to the pale amber of old photographs, and I have learned that transformation is never as dramatic as we imagine it to be. It happens in increments so small they seem invisible until suddenly, unmistakably, everything has changed.

I want to write about persistence, but not the grand persistence of heroes in stories, the kind that scales mountains or survives against impossible odds. I want to write about the persistence of small things, the quiet continuance of ordinary objects and habits and moments that somehow, against all probability, keep existing. The coffee mug with the chip in its rim that you never replace. The particular sound of a specific floorboard creaking underfoot. The way certain memories keep surfacing without invitation, neither welcome nor fully unwelcome, simply present, like the faint smell of rain that lingers in clothes dried indoors.

Consider the houseplant that sits on my windowsill, a pothos I inherited from a friend who moved across the country six years ago. I am not a good caretaker of plants. I forget to water it for weeks, then overcompensate with drowning floods. It has lived through a winter when my radiator hissed constantly and the air was dry enough to crack skin, through summers when the sun beat through the glass with what felt like personal animosity. Yet it persists. It drops leaves sometimes, grows leggy and sparse in sections, but it keeps producing new growth, pale and tender, unfurling from itself with what I can only describe as patience. I do not know if plants can be said to possess patience, but I know that this one has outlasted my neglect, my intermittent attention, my assumption that it would eventually surrender like so many others before it.

There is something humbling about being outlasted by a plant. It suggests that persistence is not necessarily a virtue, not something earned through effort or will, but simply a quality that some things possess, a way of being in time that does not require narrative or justification. The pothos does not persist to teach me a lesson, though I have learned from it nonetheless. It persists because that is what it does, what it is, what it cannot help but be.

I think often about the objects that surround us, the material culture of our daily lives that we rarely examine with any attention. The spoon that fits your hand in a way no other spoon quite does. The particular angle of light that enters your kitchen at four in the afternoon during October. The scuff mark on the doorframe that you stopped noticing years ago but that remains, a record of some hurried moment now irretrievable. These things do not ask to be meaningful, yet they accumulate meaning through sheer duration, through the simple fact of having been present while we lived our lives in their vicinity.

I remember visiting my grandmother's house after she died, the way the rooms felt both emptied and impossibly full. She had lived in that house for forty-three years, and every drawer contained evidence of her attention, her preferences, her particular way of moving through the world. Rubber bands saved in a jar. Notes written in her cramped, increasingly shaky handwriting. A collection of recipe cards stained with the evidence of use, the vanilla always measured with a certain generosity, the salt with a certain restraint. I sat on her couch, which smelled as it always had, and I understood that I was sitting in the presence of persistence, of a life that had left its marks on everything it touched.

The house was sold, eventually. The new owners renovated, painted, replaced the worn carpet with hardwood floors. I drove past once, years later, and the exterior was different, the garden my grandmother had tended with such devotion now simplified into something low-maintenance and neat. Yet I knew that the house still stood on its foundation, that the walls still contained the space where she had lived, even if every surface had been altered. There is a persistence to place that transcends ownership, that exists in the relationship between a structure and the ground it occupies, in the way light falls through windows regardless of who stands there to receive it.

I have been thinking about the persistence of certain sounds, too. The particular quality of rain on different surfaces—on a metal roof, on broad leaves, on the pavement of a street that slopes just enough to create rivulets. The way a house settles at night, the small pops and ticks of materials adjusting to temperature, sounds that become familiar enough to be soothing rather than startling. I grew up in a house with a grandfather clock in the hallway, and I can still summon the exact quality of its ticking, the way it filled the quiet hours with something like companionship, a regularity that seemed to promise continuity. The clock is long gone, sold in an estate sale, but the sound persists in me, available for recall in moments when I need the comfort of something measured and predictable.

There is persistence in language, too, in the phrases we inherit and repeat without fully understanding their origins. My mother used to say "six of one, half dozen of the other" when presented with two equivalent options, and I find myself using it now, though I cannot remember when I consciously decided to adopt it. It simply arrived in my speech, as these things do, carried across generations like a seed that found fertile ground. I wonder what other people's phrases persist in me, what words I use that were given to me by teachers, by friends, by strangers whose names I never knew. Language is perhaps the most persistent thing we have, the way it outlives individual speakers and continues to mean, to function, to connect.

I want to write about the persistence of grief, because it does not behave as we are told it will. There is no linear progression, no clean resolution. Instead, grief persists in forms that change without disappearing, that surface unexpectedly in the smell of a particular detergent, in the sight of someone walking with a gait that resembles one you knew. I have learned not to call this persistence a problem, not to pathologize what seems to me now simply a feature of having loved something that ended. The grief persists because the love persists, because what we felt was real and does not require our permission to continue existing in us.

There is a difference, I think, between persistence and stubbornness, though they can look similar from outside. Stubbornness resists, pushes against, refuses to yield. Persistence simply continues, moves forward without the need for opposition. The river that wears down stone is not stubborn; it is persistent, following gravity and its own nature, becoming itself through time and pressure. I have tried to learn this distinction, to recognize when I am being stubborn, clinging to something out of fear or pride, and when I am being persistent, continuing because continuation is the truest expression of what I am.

I have been reading about deep time, the geological scale that makes human history a thin layer, almost invisible against the vastness of planetary formation. On this scale, everything we build is temporary, yet everything we build is also part of a longer persistence, the materials recycled through endless processes, the atoms rearranged but never destroyed. The plastic we produce will persist in forms we did not intend, breaking down into particles that enter waterways, that enter bodies, that will outlast the civilizations that created them. This is not the persistence I want to celebrate, but I cannot ignore it. We are learning, slowly and painfully, that our power to create exceeds our power to control, that persistence without wisdom becomes not a virtue but a haunting.

Yet I return to the small things, the ones that seem manageable, comprehensible, almost bearable in their scale. The way my neighbor's cat appears each morning at the same time, waiting for the treat it knows will come. The particular shade of blue that appears in the sky for perhaps ten minutes on certain evenings in late summer, a blue that seems to contain all the sadness and all the hope of the season. The sound of a train whistle at night, distant enough to be melodic, close enough to be present. These persistences do not ask anything of me except attention, and I am trying to become more generous with my attention, to notice more, to let the world in its ordinary manifestations matter.

I have a friend who collects stones from every place she visits. Not precious stones, not interesting in any conventional sense—just stones that caught her attention, that seemed to want to be kept. She arranges them on a windowsill, and they sit there, persistent in their stoneness, carrying the weight of specific moments without demanding interpretation. I have started doing this too, though I am less disciplined, my stones scattered in pockets, on desks, in the bottom of bags. Each one is a small persistence, a refusal to let a place be entirely lost to time. I pick up a stone from a beach in Maine, gray and smooth, and I am back there, the cold water, the particular quality of east coast light, the feeling of being temporarily outside my ordinary life.

The body persists in ways we do not choose, carrying marks of experiences we would rather forget. The scar on my knee from a fall at sixteen. The way my back tightens in cold weather, remembering an injury that happened years ago. The sudden memory that surfaces in dreams, the body processing what the mind cannot quite integrate. I used to resent this persistence, wanted to be free of physical reminders, to exist as pure present. Now I am more willing to be a palimpsest, to let my body carry its history visibly, to understand that the persistence of these marks is also the persistence of having lived, of being someone who did things, went places, took risks, survived.

There is a kind of writing that tries to be definitive, to resolve, to conclude. I find I am less interested in this now than I used to be. I want writing that persists, that continues to mean in ways I did not anticipate, that rewards return rather than exhausting itself in a single reading. The books I love most are the ones I have lived with, that have changed as I have changed, that seem to contain more than their pages should be able to hold. I think of Virginia Woolf's *To the Lighthouse*, which I first read too young to understand, and which I have returned to at different ages, finding each time something I was not ready for before. The book persists, unchanged on my shelf, yet my experience of it is always new, a collaboration between text and reader that continues as long as I continue to open it.

I want to write about the persistence of hope, though I know this is dangerous territory, easily sentimental, easily false. I do not mean the hope that everything will be fine, that suffering will be rewarded, that the arc of the universe bends toward justice. I mean something smaller, more like the pothos on my windowsill, more like the quality of persistence itself. The hope that continues not because it is justified but because it is a habit of mind, a way of facing the day that has become as automatic as breathing. Some mornings I wake without it, and those days are harder, grayer, more purely endured. But it returns, uninvited, unexpected, as persistent as the light that follows darkness not because it has won some victory but simply because that is what light does, what it cannot help but do.

I am aware, writing this, that I have not said anything definitive, that I have circled around my subject without quite landing. But this feels appropriate to persistence, which is not a destination but a manner of traveling. The river does not arrive; it continues. The plant does not achieve; it grows. The sound of the clock does not resolve; it ticks, and ticks, and ticks, marking time without consuming it. I am trying to learn this, to be less concerned with where I am going and more attentive to how I am moving, to the quality of my persistence, to the small things that surround me and outlast me and will continue in forms I cannot imagine.

The sky is light now, the silence of early morning giving way to the sounds of a day beginning. Somewhere, a door closes. Somewhere, a kettle begins to whistle. The pothos on my windowsill receives the first direct light, and I watch as the leaves seem to shift, to orient themselves, to continue their patient work of becoming. I will water it today, or I will forget and water it tomorrow, or next week. It will persist regardless, as it has persisted, as small things do, without drama, without demand, simply present, simply continuing, simply being the exact thing that it is in the exact place where it finds itself. This is enough. This is more than enough. This is everything I know about how to keep going, written in the only language I have, offered without guarantee, without conclusion, without end.
